hypothesis: Measure the current partitioned scheduler with diagnostic-only timestamps at CPU-L 1794 MHz/1000 mV and CPU-B 2002 MHz/1050 mV. Reference sequence and unchanged ordering: docs/designs/scheduler-latency-measurement.md#the-reference-sequence-preserves-task-ownership-and-interrupt-ordering. The timing-only image returns normally on port 3-1 with all eight cores sampled and no fault record. Every memory-worker self-suspend has ordered reference, publication, drain and slice timestamps; the longest drain retains every consumed record. CPU0 alone contributes timer intervals. Each retained wait has validated holder and ticket data or an explicit unknown cause. The known task-wake and interrupt-mask targets remain unmet: recording adds work and does not shorten a scheduler path. Task-lock waits and startup masking are observations, with no claimed reduction; startup is measured before top clocks and ends at context-restore entry. The run provides no p99.99 claim from 128 busy wakes per core. Worked native budget: boot/clock readiness 3 s + workload deadline 12 s + return reserve 5 s = 20 s, below finish_by 55 s and session lifetime 60 s, leaving 35 s before finish_by. Controller wait loops publish progress each 1 ms tick; any 3 s progress gap fails. Host reset/DRAM and upload are outside the native lifetime; budget 10 s preparation, 20 s native, 5 s capture/rail restoration, total 35 s. The longest physical operation must remain supervised and a failure ends this stage without retry.

The five scheduler cases pass on the historical instruction-counter harness. Optional MTTCG/A55 conditions expose unresolved timeout, object-lock and wake-count failures in scheduler code that is instruction-equivalent to the baseline; these are retained and do not establish a diagnostic regression.
